chess.The board: Find the letter along the bottom first, then count up the numbers on the side. e4 is column e, row 4.
chess.How pieces move: Rooks go straight, bishops go diagonally, a queen does both, a king steps one square, and a knight jumps in an L. Pick a piece up and the dots show where it can go.
chess.Capturing: A piece takes by landing on an enemy square, along the way it normally moves. Pawns are the exception: they move straight but take one square diagonally forward.
chess.Check and checkmate: Check means the king is attacked. There are three ways out: move the king, block the line, or take the attacker. If none of them works, that is checkmate.
chess.Forks: A fork is one piece attacking two at once. Look for a square your piece can reach that touches both targets. Knights are especially good at this.
chess.Mate in one: List every check you can give, then test each one: can the king step away, can anything block, can anything take the checker? If all three are no, that's the move.
chess.Free pieces: Before taking, count who guards the piece. If nothing defends it, it is free. If it is defended, compare what you win with what you give up.
chess.Pins: A pin holds a piece in place because moving it would expose something bigger behind it. Look along straight lines and diagonals for two enemy pieces in a row.
chess.Skewers: A skewer is a pin the other way round: the big piece is in front, has to move, and the one behind it falls. Look for lines through the king or queen.
chess.Back-rank mates: A king behind its own pawns has no way out. A rook or queen landing on that back row can be checkmate, if nothing can block or take it.
chess.Mate in two: Start with the move that forces a reply: usually a check. Then ask what the only answer is, and find the mate after it.
chess.Discovered attacks: Move one piece out of the way and the piece behind it attacks along the opened line. The piece that moved gets a free threat of its own.
chess.Double check: Two pieces give check at once. Nothing can block both or take both, so the king has to move, which makes the king very easy to chase.
chess.Trapped pieces: Look at where the enemy piece can go. If every square it can reach is covered, it can't escape, so attack it and it falls.
chess.Deflection: Find the piece doing an important job, like guarding a square. Force it to move away, then use the job it left behind.
chess.Attraction: Offer something on a square that drags a piece, often the king, to where you want it. Then the follow-up works because of where it now stands.
chess.Promotion: Clear the way for your pawn. Often a sacrifice or a check gains the one move it needs to reach the last row and become a queen.
chess.Mate in three: Work forwards with forcing moves only: checks first, then captures. After each one, ask what replies are possible. Few replies means an easy line to follow.

maths.Mental maths: Make the sum easier first. Round one number to a ten, work that out, then fix up what you changed. 38 + 5 is 40 + 3.
maths.Percentages: Percent means out of 100. 10% is dividing by 10, 50% is halving, and 25% is halving twice. Build other percentages from those.
maths.Fractions you can see: The bottom number says how many equal parts there are. The top says how many you have. Picture the bar, then compare the shaded parts.

japanese.Vowels: There are five to learn: a, i, u, e, o. Each kana has one sound. Say it out loud and picture its story, then try the kana again.
japanese.K and S: Each row is one consonant in front of the five vowels: ka ki ku ke ko, sa shi su se so. Find the vowel you know, then add the consonant.
japanese.First words: Read one kana at a time, then join the sounds together. Each kana is one beat, so a word's length tells you how many sounds it has.

coding.Step by step: I do one block at a time, in order. Put your finger on me and walk the steps yourself. Where do you end up?
coding.Loops: Count the squares in one straight run. That's the number of repeats. Blocks inside the repeat all run, in order, once each time round.
coding.If and else: I check the look before each step. If it's true I do the first part, and if it isn't I do the else part. Try it one square at a time.
coding.Nested loops: Work from the inside out. Do the inner loop in full, then count that as one go of the outer loop. Inner times outer is the total.
coding.Repeat until: Before each round I check the condition. When it's true, I stop. If nothing inside gets me closer to it, I'd go round for ever.
coding.Your own block: A new block is a plan with a name. Writing the plan doesn't run it: calling its name does. Read the plan first, then follow each call.
coding.Parameters: A parameter is a gap in your block that gets filled when you call it. hop(3) puts 3 wherever the plan says n.
coding.Variables: A variable is a named number. Set puts a value in it and change adds to it. Keep your own running count as you follow me.
coding.Comparisons and logic: A comparison is a question with a yes or no answer. And needs both parts to be yes. Or needs just one. Not swaps the answer.
coding.Lists: A loop over a list runs once per value, in order. Each time round, its name holds the next value. Say each value as you go.
coding.Drawing: Every square I stand on gets painted. Find the shape's repeating part first: that is the inside of your loop.
coding.Find the bug: Watch where I go wrong. The bug is usually the block just before that spot. Change only that one, then follow the plan again.
coding.From blocks to code: It's the same plan in different clothes. A for line is a repeat, its braces hold the inside, and each line ending in a semicolon is one step.

javascript.Printing: console.log prints what is in its brackets. Text goes in quote marks, numbers and sums don't. A comparison prints true or false.
javascript.Variables: A name holds a value. let makes one that can change, const one that can't. Reading a name gives its newest value, line by line from the top.
javascript.Text: + glues text with no space added. .length counts letters, and places start at 0, so the first letter is [0].
javascript.Conditions: Read the test on its own first: is it true right now? True runs the first { }, false runs the else if there is one. && needs both sides, || needs one.
javascript.Loops: Say each round out loud: what is i, does the test hold, what prints? A for starts at 0 and stops before the number, so i < 3 is three rounds.
javascript.Functions: Writing a function runs nothing. A call runs it, with the inputs filled in. return hands one value back to where the call was.
javascript.Arrays: A list counts from 0, so the last place is one less than .length. .push adds to the end and for...of visits each in turn.
javascript.Objects: An object holds values under names. A dot reads one. With a list of objects, first find the one in the list, then the part.
javascript.Array methods: .map changes each and gives a new list. .filter keeps those your test says true to. .forEach only does something, and gives nothing back.
javascript.Callbacks: Pass a function by its name with no brackets. With brackets it runs right now. The function you passed to runs it when the time comes.

typescript.Annotations: The label after the colon says what a name may hold: number, string, boolean, or a list like number[]. With no label, the first value decides.
typescript.Typed functions: Label every input, and what comes back after the brackets. The checker then tests every call and every return against those labels.
typescript.Unions: A | means either. You may only use what both sides have, until a typeof or === check tells the checker which it is.
typescript.Interfaces: An interface lists the parts an object must have and what each holds. A ? part may be missing, so check it before using it.
typescript.Generics: T is a label filled in by the call. Whatever goes in decides what comes out. Read T off the argument, then read the rest with it.

testing.Your first test: test gives it a name, expect holds what the code gave, toBe says what it should be. Work the answer out from what the function is for.
testing.Catching bugs: Ask: would a wrong version give the same answer for these values? If it would, pick others. 2 and 2 can't tell adding from multiplying.
testing.Edges: Bugs gather at lines. If the code says >= 18, test exactly 18 and just under. Try empty lists and zero too.
testing.Lists and objects: toBe asks if it is the very same thing, so two equal lists fail it. toEqual compares the insides. toContain asks if one thing is in there.
testing.Errors: expect gets a plan to run, () => pos(-1), so the error happens where toThrow can watch. Test the good road as well as the refusal.
testing.A full suite: List the roads through the code, then write one check for each, at its edge. When a faulty version gets through, the message says just what to add.
